scope.summary: The Act covers providers that place AI systems on the EU market or put them into service in the EU, wherever the provider is established, and deployers established or located in the EU.
scope.hospitalityNote: A non-EU hotel group whose AI output is used in the EU can therefore be in scope.

tiers.name: Unacceptable risk (prohibited)
tiers.description: Practices seen as a clear threat to safety, livelihoods and rights. Banned outright.
generalExamples: Manipulative or deceptive AI causing significant harm
Exploiting vulnerabilities (age, disability, social or economic situation)
Untargeted scraping of faces from the internet or CCTV
Emotion recognition in the workplace (except medical or safety reasons)
Biometric categorisation to infer race, religion, sexual orientation and similar
hospitalityExamples: A hotel using cameras or voice analysis to infer staff emotions
Pricing designed to exploit a guest's vulnerability
tiers.appliesNote: New points (ba)/(bb) on non-consensual intimate content and child sexual abuse material apply from 2 Dec 2026 (Art. 5; Art. 113).

tiers.name: High risk
tiers.description: Use cases that can seriously affect health, safety or fundamental rights. Allowed, but under strict requirements for providers (risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy, conformity assessment, registration) and duties for deployers.
routes: Route 1 (product): AI that is a safety component of a regulated product (Annex I). NARROWED by Omnibus: AI solely used for non-safety-related user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control is NOT a safety component (Art. 6(1a)) - unless its failure would endanger health and safety (Art. 6(1b)).
Route 2 (use case): stand-alone uses listed in Annex III
hospitalityExamples: AI that allocates shifts or monitors staff performance
Identifying guests at a distance by face
tiers.appliesNote: Annex III systems: 2 Dec 2027. Annex I systems: 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 113). Postponed from Aug 2026 by the Omnibus.
tiers.omnibusCorrection: Route 1 narrowed by new Art. 6(1a)-(1c) and the redefined 'safety component' in Art. 3(14).

tiers.name: Limited risk (transparency)
tiers.description: People must know when they are dealing with AI or AI-generated content.
generalExamples: Synthetic images, audio, video and text
Emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems (disclosure to the people exposed)
hospitalityExamples: AI-generated photos or videos of the property
tiers.appliesNote: Providers of content generators already on the market before that date have until 2 Dec 2026 for machine-readable marking (Art. 111(4)).

tiers.name: Minimal or no risk
tiers.description: No AI-Act-specific obligations. The Commission says most AI used in the EU falls here. Voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.

crossCuttingDuty.name: AI literacy
crossCuttingDuty.description: All providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and others operating AI on their behalf.
crossCuttingDuty.omnibusChange: Art. 4 was replaced in full. The duty is retained and now expressly does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. The Commission must publish practical compliance examples on the single information platform, and the Board must adopt recommendations setting common objectives.
crossCuttingDuty.penaltyNote: AI literacy (Art. 4) is NOT among the obligations listed in Art. 99(4), so it carries no direct fine cap under that paragraph.
crossCuttingDuty.omnibusCorrection: Article replaced, not merely amended; the Commission and Board duties are new.

classificationFilter.name: The Art. 6(3) filter
classificationFilter.summary: An Annex III system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk and only does one of four narrow things.
escapeConditions: Improves the result of a completed human activity
Detects patterns without replacing human assessment
classificationFilter.override: Any Annex III system that profiles natural persons is ALWAYS high-risk.
classificationFilter.documentationDuty: A provider relying on the filter must document its assessment and register the system (Art. 6(4); Art. 49(2)).
classificationFilter.guidanceStatus: Commission guidelines on high-risk classification published in draft 19 May 2026; consultation closed 23 July 2026; final version pending.

gpai.name: General-purpose AI models
gpai.positionInRegime: Outside the pyramid. Regulates the model makers, not the hotels using them.
providerDuties: Pass information to downstream system builders
gpai.hospitalityNote: Hotels are only affected if they substantially modify such a model (see providerSwitchRoutes route E).

aiAct.cap: EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher

aiAct.breach: Provider duties (Art. 16), deployer duties (Art. 26), transparency (Art. 50), provider-switch duties (Art. 25(2),(4), now expressly listed at Art. 99(4)(da))
Incorrect or misleading information to authorities

aiAct.cap: Each cap applies at whichever amount is LOWER
Lower-amount rule for Art. 99(4) and (5) only, not for prohibitions

gdpr.breach: Controller/processor duties such as DPIAs and security

enforcement.summary: Enforcement is shared between the Commission's AI Office and national market surveillance authorities. Anyone can file a complaint with a market surveillance authority.
enforcement.gap: National layer researched on 10 Nov 2026 for the six focus countries (France, Germany, Spain, Sweden, UK, Switzerland): see nationalLayer. Designations in France, Spain and Sweden are still provisional.

penalties.omnibusCorrection: Art. 99(1) replaced: penalties may include warnings and non-monetary measures, and Member States must take the interests and economic viability of SMEs, start-ups and SMCs into account when imposing them. Art. 99(4)(da) and Art. 99(6a) are new.

provider.name: Provider
provider.legalDefinition: Anyone who develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge.
provider.keyPoint: Putting into service includes supplying a system for own use in the Union. You do not have to sell the system to be its provider.

deployer.name: Deployer
deployer.legalDefinition: Anyone using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity.
deployer.keyPoint: Covers any professional use, including by employees acting for the hotel.

roles.note: A hotel is usually a deployer and can also be a provider of the same system. In both roles it is also an employer, which matters for the high-risk employment rules (Annex III, point 4) and for staff literacy.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Risk management
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: A continuous, documented risk-management process across the lifecycle.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Data governance
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: Relevant, representative, as error-free as possible data, with bias assessment and mitigation. Now cross-refers to Art. 4a(1) for any processing of special categories for bias detection; former para 5 deleted.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Technical documentation
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: Drawn up before use, containing at minimum the Annex IV elements. SMEs, start-ups and SMCs may use a Commission simplified form, which notified bodies must accept.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Human oversight
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: Humans can monitor, interpret, override or stop the system.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: The system must be accurate, robust and secure.

highRiskProviderRequirements.name: Quality management system
highRiskProviderRequirements.oneLine: Implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, in particular for SMEs, start-ups and SMCs, without lowering the required rigour or level of protection.
highRiskProviderRequirements.omnibusCorrection: Para 2 replaced - new proportionality relief, absent from the source briefing.

provider: Must not place on the market or put into service (Art. 5)
Quality management system, proportionate to organisation size for SMEs, start-ups and SMCs (Art. 17(2))
Conformity assessment before use; for Annex III points 2-8, including employment, this is internal control without a notified body (Art. 43(2))
Serious-incident reporting within 15 days at the latest, or 2 or 10 days in specific cases (Art. 73)
deployer: Ensure input data under its control is relevant and representative
Monitor, suspend use and inform the provider or authority if risks appear
Keep logs for at least 6 months
As employer, inform workers' representatives and affected workers BEFORE use (Art. 26(7))
Use provider information for the GDPR data protection impact assessment
Affected persons have a right to an explanation of decisions (Art. 86)
obligationsByRoleAndTier.omnibusCorrection: Art. 17 proportionality added; Art. 25(2)/(4) duties are now expressly fineable under Art. 99(4)(da).

provider: Design chatbots so people know they are talking to AI, unless obvious (Art. 50(1))
Mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in machine-readable form (Art. 50(2))
deployer: Disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless human-reviewed with editorial responsibility
Inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation (Art. 50(3)-(4))
Disclosure must be clear, at the latest at first interaction or exposure, and accessible (Art. 50(5))

providerSwitchRoutes.name: Build it yourself
providerSwitchRoutes.whatHappens: Developing a system, or having one developed, and putting it into service under your own name, including for own use, makes you the provider.
providerSwitchRoutes.hotelExample: A chain codes its own guest assistant on top of an LLM API. The chain is provider of the system; the LLM company remains provider of the model. The Act calls this role a downstream provider.

providerSwitchRoutes.name: Put your brand on a high-risk system
providerSwitchRoutes.whatHappens: Deployer becomes provider of that high-risk system, unless the contract allocates obligations otherwise.
providerSwitchRoutes.hotelExample: A chain rebrands a vendor's recruitment tool as [Brand] Talent AI.

providerSwitchRoutes.name: Substantially modify a high-risk system
providerSwitchRoutes.whatHappens: A change not foreseen in the original conformity assessment that affects compliance or the intended purpose; the system stays high-risk.
providerSwitchRoutes.hotelExample: IT retrains a vendor's candidate-scoring model on its own hiring data and changes the scoring logic.

providerSwitchRoutes.name: Change the intended purpose so the system becomes high-risk
providerSwitchRoutes.whatHappens: Using a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose system, for a high-risk purpose.
providerSwitchRoutes.hotelExample: HR uses a general chatbot to rank applicants or evaluate staff. This can happen informally - see shadow AI.
providerSwitchRoutes.flag: Most common accidental route in hospitality.

providerSwitchRoutes.name: Significantly modify a GPAI model
providerSwitchRoutes.whatHappens: Becomes provider of the modified model only if the change significantly alters its generality, capabilities or systemic risk. The indicative threshold is modification compute above one third of the original model's training compute. The Commission says few modifications currently meet it.
providerSwitchRoutes.hotelExample: Fine-tuning a model on brand voice is almost certainly not enough to become a GPAI model provider, but you are still provider of the system built around it (route A).

switchConsequences.summary: The original provider is no longer the provider of that specific system. It must closely cooperate with the new provider, which now expressly includes: (a) technical documentation sufficient to assess Art. 16 compliance; (b) informing the new provider of known limitations and failure modes; and (c) targeted technical access, including for testing and validation.
switchConsequences.carveOut: Does not apply where the initial provider clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk system.
switchConsequences.openSourceCarveOut: Art. 25(4): the written-agreement duty between a high-risk provider and third-party suppliers does NOT apply to third parties making tools, services, processes or components publicly available under a free and open-source licence, other than general-purpose AI models.
switchConsequences.penaltyNote: Art. 99(4)(da) now expressly lists Art. 25(2) and (4) duties among the Tier 2 fineable obligations.
switchConsequences.omnibusCorrection: Cooperation duty enumerated; open-source carve-out and the Art. 99(4)(da) fine hook are new.

boundaries.name: Prototyping is outside the Act
boundaries.detail: Research, testing and development before a system is placed on the market or put into service are excluded. Testing in real-world conditions is NOT excluded.

boundaries.name: Legacy high-risk systems
boundaries.detail: High-risk systems already placed on the market or in service before 2 Dec 2027 are covered only if their design changes significantly from that date. Public-authority users have until 2 Aug 2030. Prohibitions apply regardless.
boundaries.caution: Buying or building now is not automatically grandfathered forever: any significant update after that date brings the tool into scope.

boundaries.name: Real-world testing has its own regime
boundaries.detail: Testing in real-world conditions was already outside the Art. 2(8) exclusion. The Omnibus amended Art. 60 and inserted a new Art. 60a for real-world testing of high-risk AI covered by Annex I Section B harmonisation legislation outside AI regulatory sandboxes, supervised under Art. 76(1).
boundaries.omnibusCorrection: New Art. 60a, absent from the source briefing.

hospitalityHeadline: Nothing is high-risk because it happens in a hotel. Most guest-facing and commercial AI sits in the minimal or transparency tiers. The real exposure lies in (1) the hotel as employer, (2) biometrics, (3) transparency towards guests, and (4) the builder trap.

hospitalityProvisions.whyItMatters: Non-EU groups with EU guests or properties are in scope.
Front office, revenue, HR, marketing and F&B staff using AI need proportionate training.
Pricing or upselling designed to exploit a guest who cannot compare, or a vulnerable group. Normal demand-based pricing is not covered.
Banned for staff, e.g. analysing agents' voices or front-desk faces for mood.

Booking chatbots, WhatsApp concierges, voice agents; AI-generated property imagery. Final Commission guidelines (5 Nov 2026): disclose at the first turn or start of the call, with reminders in long calls; terms and conditions alone are insufficient; customer and helpdesk chatbots never qualify as obvious; internal assistants for trained staff do (paras 37-38, 45). An AI image that misleads about the property's real appearance is a deep fake and must be labelled, and the label does not cure misleading advertising. AI-written sustainability, health or consumer-safety claims published to the public need a label unless substantively human-reviewed under someone's editorial responsibility (paras 131-136). The Art. 111(2) grandfathering does not cover Art. 50.

Recognising guests at a distance (e.g. VIP or banned-guest recognition on lobby cameras) is high-risk, also on private property. 1:1 face verification at check-in and opt-in access control are excluded from Annex III but are still special-category data under GDPR. Emotion recognition of guests from biometric data is high-risk, not banned: the draft guidelines' example is call-centre AI reading callers' emotions from their voice to route angry callers (p. 37). Voiceprint recognition of returning callers without their active involvement is remote identification.

Recruitment (targeted job ads, application filtering, candidate evaluation); decisions on terms, promotion, termination; task allocation based on individual behaviour or traits; performance and behaviour monitoring. Hospitality is labour-intensive with high seasonal hiring, which makes this the most likely high-risk exposure.
hospitalityProvisions.flag: Most likely high-risk exposure for hotels.

hospitalityProvisions.whyItMatters: Workers' representatives and affected staff must be informed before a high-risk system is used at work. Member States may keep stricter worker-protection laws.
Chains with in-house tech teams, white-labelled vendor tools, or staff repurposing general AI for HR.
Many independents are SMEs; lower fine caps and simplified documentation.

notHighRisk.headline: Room, menu or table pricing is not in Annex III.
notHighRisk.detail: The only pricing listed is life and health insurance (Annex III, 5(c)). Pricing based on identified customers still triggers GDPR.
notHighRisk.recommendedPractice: Document pricing inputs and test whether changing one personal variable changes the price.

gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: Guests or staff may not be subject to purely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, except under contract, law or explicit consent, and then with a right to human intervention.
gdprLayer.example: A chatbot automatically refusing complaint credits or upgrades.

gdprLayer.provision: GDPR Art. 35: data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: Required for systematic profiling with significant effects, large-scale special-category data (e.g. biometrics, health or dietary needs), or large-scale monitoring of public areas.

gdprLayer.provision: AI Act Art. 4a (NEW) x GDPR special categories
gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: Providers of high-risk systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), subject to six cumulative conditions: no viable alternative data including synthetic or anonymised; technical re-use limits plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation; strict documented access controls; no onward transmission or third-party access; deletion once bias is corrected or retention ends; and documented necessity in the records of processing. Art. 4a(2) extends the option to deployers of high-risk systems and to other systems, while creating no obligation to perform bias detection.
gdprLayer.whyItMattersHere: This is the bridge between the two regimes. A hotel building or deploying CV screening that wants to test for bias across protected characteristics now has an express AI Act route, with GDPR-grade conditions attached. Art. 10(5), the former home of this permission, is deleted.
gdprLayer.omnibusCorrection: New article, absent from the source briefing.

gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: AI vendors processing guest data need a processor contract with GDPR guarantees.

Status on 10 Nov 2026: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework is still valid. The Latombe appeal (C-703/25 P) is pending at the Court of Justice. The US Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling (29 Jun 2026) allows the President to remove FTC members at will, which undermines a premise of the framework. noyb asked the Commission to repeal it on 30 Jun 2026.
gdprLayer.prudentPosture: Keep standard contractual clauses (SCCs) and transfer impact assessments (TIAs) as a fallback; prefer EU-hosted AI for sensitive data.

gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: Member States may set specific rules for employee data, including recruitment and work organisation.
gdprLayer.gap: National labour rules on workplace AI researched on 10 Nov 2026 for the six focus countries: see nationalLayer.

gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: A model is only anonymous if identification or extraction of personal data is very unlikely. Unlawfully trained models can taint lawful deployment.
Breaches must be notified to the authority within 72 hours where feasible.

gdprLayer.provision: AI Act Art. 27: fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)
gdprLayer.hotelRelevance: Art. 27(1) binds only three categories of deployer: bodies governed by public law; private entities providing public services; and deployers of Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) systems. Annex III point 2 systems are excluded entirely.
gdprLayer.whatThisMeansForHotels: An ordinary hotel owes NO FRIA for its main high-risk exposure. Employment systems sit in Annex III point 4, which is not in Art. 27's scope, so CV screening, shift allocation and performance monitoring trigger Art. 26 deployer duties and a GDPR DPIA but not a FRIA. The one hotel case that does trigger it is deploying creditworthiness evaluation or credit scoring of natural persons, which is Annex III point 5(b) - for example credit scoring of a natural person for access to a financial or other essential service. The draft guidelines limit 5(b) to essential private services, so scoring guests for deposits on hotel stays is most likely outside it (paras 301-304). Life and health insurance pricing (5(c)) is not a hotel activity. Narrowed further by the draft classification guidelines: corporate-account credit assessment is outside Annex III 5(b) even where an individual owner backs the loan, because the company is the primary beneficiary. The trigger is scoring an individual guest or a sole trader in their own right.
gdprLayer.omnibusChange: Art. 27(4) now allows the FRIA to cross-refer to, or incorporate parts of, a GDPR Art. 35 DPIA where the obligations overlap. Art. 27(5) requires the AI Office to develop a questionnaire template, possibly as an automated tool, to help deployers comply in a simplified manner.

scenarios.title: Vendor chatbot or WhatsApp concierge for bookings and FAQs
obligations: Vendor designs AI disclosure; hotel checks it is switched on and clear
Promotional messages count as direct marketing under ePrivacy
scenarios.consequences: AI Act Tier 2 for transparency breaches, falling on whoever holds the duty; GDPR fines; contractual liability for promises the bot made.

scenarios.title: AI-generated photos or videos of rooms and views in marketing
scenarios.classification: Limited risk if a deepfake (Art. 50(4); definition Art. 3(60))
obligations: Disclose realistic AI imagery at first exposure
scenarios.consequences: AI Act Tier 2; consumer-law exposure; reputation.

scenarios.title: Revenue management system with dynamic pricing
scenarios.consequences: GDPR if personal data is used; AI Act Tier 1 only in the extreme exploitation case.
scenarios.aiActTierNote: Tier 1 only in the extreme exploitation case; otherwise no AI Act fine exposure.

scenarios.title: Vendor CV-screening or candidate-ranking tool for seasonal hiring
scenarios.consequences: AI Act Tier 2; GDPR (Art. 22 automated rejection); discrimination claims.
scenarios.omnibusCorrection: Bias testing across protected characteristics now has an express route: Art. 4a permits exceptional processing of special categories for bias detection and correction under six conditions. Art. 10(5) is deleted.

scenarios.title: Workforce software that allocates shifts by individual performance or tracks housekeeping productivity
scenarios.classification: High risk if allocating tasks by behaviour, ratings or traits, monitoring performance, or significantly changing working hours or deciding leave (Annex III, 4(b)). Allocation on stated availability alone is outside the task-allocation limb (draft guidelines paras 271-272). The Art. 6(3) filter is unlikely to help because it profiles.
obligations: As D4, especially informing workers' representatives first (Art. 26(7))
scenarios.consequences: AI Act Tier 2; GDPR; labour-law disputes.
scenarios.note: Shifts allocated only on stated availability, required accreditation or location rely on objective criteria and fall outside the task-allocation limb of 4(b) (draft Annex III guidelines paras 271-272). Allocation using punctuality, reliability, shift acceptance or customer/manager ratings is high-risk; the Commission's worked example of a retail scheduler using these inputs is high-risk with no Art. 6(3) escape (p. 76). Tracking output speed or tasks completed is performance monitoring (para 275). Significant changes to regular working hours and leave decisions stay within 4(b) regardless (e3).

scenarios.title: Face verification at self check-in (1:1) vs VIP recognition on lobby cameras
scenarios.classification: 1:1 verification: outside Annex III but GDPR Art. 9. Remote identification: high risk (Annex III, 1(a)).
obligations: Explicit consent or GDPR Art. 9 basis
For remote identification, the full Art. 26 duties
scenarios.consequences: GDPR EUR 20m/4% tier (Art. 9); AI Act Tier 2.
scenarios.note: Draft Annex III guidelines: 1:1 verification against a passport chip, ID card, device, or a database encrypted with a key held only by the person is outside high-risk (para 136). Access control where a registered person consciously presents themselves is not remote, even when matched one-to-many against the list of registered people (paras 138, 140; examples p. 25); merely informing people of cameras is not active involvement (para 140). CCTV identifying people on private property is remote biometric identification; point 1(a) is not limited to publicly accessible spaces (p. 24). GDPR Art. 9 applies in every case.

scenarios.title: Call-centre tool scoring agents' emotions from their voice
obligations: Do not use. Text-only sentiment analysis of guest messages is NOT emotion recognition because it does not use biometric data (Art. 3(39)).

scenarios.title: Chain's IT team builds its own guest assistant via an LLM API (with PMS/CRM connectors)
obligations: Design AI disclosure into the product (Art. 50(1))
Machine-readable marking if it generates content (Art. 50(2))
GDPR: the API vendor as processor, transfers
scenarios.consequences: AI Act Tier 2; GDPR transfer fines (EUR 20m/4% tier).
scenarios.omnibusCorrection: Art. 25(4): no written-agreement duty towards third parties supplying tools, services, processes or components under a free and open-source licence, other than GPAI models.

scenarioTimingNuance: A high-risk tool already in use before 2 Dec 2027 is only caught if its design changes significantly afterwards (Art. 111(2)). Buying or building now is not automatically grandfathered forever.

shadowAI.definition: Any AI tool used for work without the organisation's knowledge or approval. It also includes AI that enters through vendor updates or embedded features without a deliberate decision to buy AI.
howItOccurs: Personal chatbot accounts, e.g. a reservations agent pasting a group rooming list into a free chatbot to draft a confirmation email
Browser extensions on shared front-desk PCs, meeting note-takers, free translation or writing tools, accounts registered with personal emails
Embedded or vendor AI: new AI features in Microsoft 365, CRM or PMS; a vendor adding AI without notice; an agency processing guest data with AI
shadowAI.rootCause: Approved routes are slow (e.g. waiting three days for a translation), and blanket bans push use underground.

scale.caveat: Cross-industry figures. No hospitality-specific shadow-AI survey found - this is a gap the SBP interviews could fill.

findings.finding: Used AI despite believing it was against policy
findings.source: PagerDuty / Wakefield, Apr 2026, 1,250 office workers at $500m+ firms in AU, JP, UK, US

findings.finding: Entered customer data into public AI tools
findings.figure: 34% (40% at firms with fewer than 1,500 staff)

findings.finding: Would rather hide AI use than ask
Adopted AI tools without employer approval

whyHotelsSpecifically: Data hotels hold is sensitive: VIP profiles with medical and dietary needs, incident reports, passport details, personnel and disciplinary records. Health and biometric data are special categories under GDPR.
A paste is a data transfer, often to non-EU servers, with no record of what was shared.

AI Act link: shadow use can silently turn the hotel into a provider of a high-risk system (scenario P3, Art. 25(1)(c)). It also undermines AI literacy duties (Art. 4) and transparency duties (Art. 50).
Fragmented structure: franchisors, owners, operators and vendors all touch hotel data, which makes oversight harder.

regulatory: Unlawful processing or transfer can fall under the GDPR's EUR 20m/4% tier (GDPR Art. 83)
A leak can be a personal data breach requiring notification within 72 hours where feasible (GDPR Art. 33)
Possible AI Act Tier 2 exposure via Arts. 25, 26, 50 (Art. 99)
consequences.commercial: A team leader pasted a guest complaint into a public chatbot, and the generated letter promised an unapproved GBP 75 credit. The guest escalated to the GM, turning a recoverable service failure into a reputational and commercial liability.
consequences.confidentiality: Samsung banned generative AI tools in 2023 after staff uploaded sensitive source code to ChatGPT.
consequences.governance: With no AI register, a hotel cannot answer a guest asking how their data was used.

whatWorks: AI register: a live list of purchased, embedded, vendor and staff-introduced AI
Amnesty, not blame: disclosure of an unapproved tool triggers an assessment, not a reprimand
Acceptable Use Policy that staff read and acknowledge, plus approved enterprise alternatives and manager review of AI-drafted guest communications
Private or internal tools instead of public chatbots for guest data
Redirect rather than slow down AI use, into governed platforms

glossary.meaning: A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions.
A model with significant generality, able to perform a wide range of distinct tasks and be integrated into many downstream systems.
Develops, or has developed, an AI system or GPAI model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name, paid or free.
Provider of an AI system that integrates an AI model, whether its own or another company's.
Uses an AI system under its authority, except for personal non-professional use.
Umbrella term: provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer or distributor.
First making available of an AI system or GPAI model on the EU market.
Supplying an AI system for first use to a deployer or for own use in the EU.
The use the provider intends, as stated in instructions, marketing and technical documentation.
Use not in line with the intended purpose but foreseeable from human behaviour.
Post-market change not foreseen in the conformity assessment that affects compliance or the intended purpose.
System that is a safety component of an Annex I product, or listed in Annex III, unless the Art. 6(3) filter applies.
Automated evaluation of personal aspects such as performance, preferences or behaviour. It makes an Annex III system always high-risk.
Automated recognition of human features to establish identity by comparison with a database.
1:1 check that a person is who they claim to be. Excluded from Annex III 1(a).
AI identifying or inferring emotions or intentions from biometric data.
AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video resembling real persons, objects, places or events that would falsely appear authentic.
Skills, knowledge and understanding to deploy AI in an informed way and be aware of its opportunities, risks and possible harm.
AI incident or malfunction leading to death or serious health harm, critical-infrastructure disruption, infringement of fundamental-rights law, or serious harm to property or the environment.
Procedure showing a high-risk system meets the requirements. For Annex III points 2-8, internal control.
Mark showing a high-risk system conforms with the Act.
Provider's ongoing collection and analysis of performance data after release.
National body enforcing the AI Act on AI systems.
Commission body supervising GPAI models and coordinating enforcement.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act. In force 27 Jul 2026; delayed high-risk dates, added prohibitions, SME/SMC relief.
Small and medium enterprise / small mid-cap enterprise (per Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099), with lighter fine caps and simplified documentation.
AI used for work without the organisation's knowledge or approval.
Inventory of all AI in use (bought, embedded, vendor- or staff-introduced) with owner, purpose and risk tier.
Data protection impact assessment, required by GDPR for high-risk processing.
EU-US adequacy arrangement for transfers to certified US companies. Valid but contested as of Nov 2026.
Standard contractual clauses / transfer impact assessment: fallback tools for non-EU transfers.

openItems.item: High-risk classification guidelines are still draft (all three documents read by 13 Nov 2026). A further AI Board consultation and stakeholder feedback round is foreseen before adoption.
No hospitality-specific shadow-AI survey found. Current figures are cross-industry office workers. This is a gap the SBP interviews could fill.
DPF: monitor the Court of Justice's ruling in Latombe (C-703/25 P) and any Commission action following Trump v. Slaughter.

Art. 2(13) is new and unresolved: requirements in Arts. 9-15 and 17-25 may be limited for Annex I high-risk systems where Section A legislation gives equivalent or higher protection. The Commission must adopt delegated acts by 2 August 2027 specifying which systems, which requirements, and the scope of the limitation. Until then the extent of this relief is unknown.

wizard.design: Short triage that skips irrelevant branches. Most paths resolve in 5 to 6 questions. Each question exposes an optional deep dive. The outcome states role, tier, obligations, applicable date, fine exposure, GDPR flags and a confidence level, and links to the matching scenarios.

questions.help: The Act covers providers placing AI on the EU market or putting it into service in the EU, wherever established, and deployers established or located in the EU.

choices.label: Yes - we are established in the EU, or we place AI on the EU market
Our group is outside the EU, but the AI output is used in the EU (EU guests or properties)
choices.note: In scope. A non-EU hotel group whose AI output is used in the EU can be caught.

choices.label: No EU nexus at all

questions.prompt: How did this system reach you?
questions.help: A hotel is usually a deployer and can also be a provider of the same system.

choices.label: A vendor supplied it and we use it as supplied
We built it, or had it built, and put it into service under our own name
choices.note: Includes supplying a system for own use. You do not have to sell it to be its provider.

choices.label: It is an internal pilot, never used live

questions.prompt: Have you done any of these to the vendor's system?
questions.help: Any one of these can make you the provider instead of the vendor.

choices.label: Put our own name or trademark on it
Used it for a different purpose than intended (e.g. a general chatbot to rank applicants)
choices.flag: Most common accidental route. See shadow AI.

choices.label: Substantially modified it (retrained it, changed its scoring logic)
None of the above

questions.prompt: Does the system do any of these?
questions.help: These are banned outright, for providers and deployers alike.

choices.label: Infers staff emotions from biometric data (voice, face) outside medical or safety reasons
Manipulates or exploits a vulnerability (age, disability, social or economic situation) causing significant harm
Social scoring, untargeted scraping of faces, or biometric categorisation inferring race, religion, sexual orientation and similar
Generates non-consensual intimate content or child sexual abuse material
None of the above

questions.prompt: What does the system actually do?
questions.help: The use case sets the tier, not the technology.

choices.label: Recruitment: targeted job ads, application filtering, candidate evaluation
Worker management: task allocation by behaviour or traits, performance or behaviour monitoring, decisions on terms, promotion or termination
Identifies people at a distance by face or other biometrics (e.g. VIP recognition on lobby cameras)
1:1 face verification at check-in (confirms a person is who they claim to be)
choices.note: Excluded from Annex III 1(a), but still special-category data under GDPR Art. 9.

choices.label: Infers guests' emotions from biometric data (e.g. voice)
choices.note: High-risk, not banned - the Art. 5 ban covers the workplace.

choices.label: Credit scoring of guests
Life or health insurance pricing
It is a safety component of a regulated product (lifts, machinery, medical devices) AND its failure would endanger health or safety
choices.note: Omnibus carve-out: if the AI is solely used for non-safety-related user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control, it is NOT a safety component (Art. 6(1a)) and this route does not apply. Most hotel building-management AI falls in the carve-out.
choices.omnibusCorrection: Label tightened and carve-out added per new Art. 6(1a)-(1b).

choices.label: None of these - guest chat, pricing, forecasting, back office

questions.prompt: Does the system profile natural persons?
questions.help: Profiling means automated evaluation of personal aspects such as performance, preferences or behaviour. If yes, the Art. 6(3) filter is unavailable and the system is always high-risk.

choices.label: Yes, it evaluates individuals
No, and it only performs a narrow procedural task, improves a completed human activity, detects patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task
choices.note: You must document the assessment and still register the system (Art. 6(4); Art. 49(2)). Commission guidelines are still draft.

choices.label: Not sure
choices.note: Treat as high-risk until the final classification guidelines land.

questions.prompt: Does the system interact with people or generate content?
questions.help: Transparency duties stack on top of the tier - a minimal-risk chatbot still owes disclosure.

choices.label: Interacts with people directly (chatbot, voice agent)
Generates synthetic image, audio, video or text
Produces deepfakes - realistic depictions of real people, places or events
Performs emotion recognition or biometric categorisation on people
None of the above

questions.help: GDPR applies in parallel and is often the bigger exposure.

choices.label: Personal data of guests or staff
Special-category data (biometric, health, dietary needs)
Solely automated decisions with legal or significant effect
Data goes to servers outside the EU
choices.note: DPF still valid but contested as of Nov 2026.

choices.label: No personal data

out-of-scope-territorial.headline: Outside the AI Act's territorial scope
out-of-scope-territorial.detail: No EU nexus. Note that output used in the EU can bring a non-EU group back into scope.

out-of-scope-prototyping.headline: Outside the Act for now
out-of-scope-prototyping.detail: Research, testing and development before placing on the market or putting into service are excluded. Testing in real-world conditions is NOT excluded, and GDPR still applies to any personal data used. Obligations kick in on first real use.

prohibited.headline: Prohibited practice - do not use
prohibited.detail: Banned outright for providers and deployers.
prohibited.fine: Tier 1: EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher

assemble.headline: Assembled from the answers
assemble.instruction: Resolve the tier from the highest-severity flag set (prohibited > high > transparency > minimal), then render: role and any Art. 25 switch route; tier with its applicable date; the matching obligation list from obligationsByRoleAndTier; any Art. 50 duties on top; GDPR flags; the fine exposure for that tier; the lowest confidence level touched on the path; and links to matching scenarios by role and tier.

annexIIIReference.purpose: Full Annex III structure as the reference layer behind the hospitality view. Areas 1, 4 and 5 carry verbatim sub-points from the June 2024 Official Journal text; the other five carry headings only, by design. Annex III was not amended by the Omnibus, so this text stands.

areas.hospitalityNote: Remote biometric identification (1(a)) and emotion recognition from biometric data (1(c)) are the live ones. 1:1 verification is excluded.
areas.headingVerbatim: Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law

subPoints.text: Remote biometric identification systems. This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be.
subPoints.hotelUse: VIP or banned-guest recognition on lobby or other CCTV is caught, including on private property (draft guidelines p. 24). Voiceprint recognition of returning callers without their active involvement is caught: a company voice database can be the reference database (paras 141, 144). 1:1 verification at self check-in (selfie against the ID document) and opt-in access control where the guest presents themselves are outside (paras 136, 138, 140), but remain GDPR Art. 9 special-category data.

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation, according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics.
subPoints.hotelUse: Inferring protected traits from biometrics is prohibited outright under Art. 5, not merely high-risk.

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used for emotion recognition.
subPoints.hotelUse: Emotion recognition of GUESTS from biometric data is high-risk here. The draft guidelines' worked example: call-centre AI analysing customers' vocal tone, pitch and volume to gauge satisfaction or route angry callers to a human (p. 37); cameras screening crowd mood are also covered. Deployers must inform everyone exposed (Art. 50(3)). Text sentiment, a mere smile, pain or fatigue are not emotion recognition (paras 124, 177). Emotion recognition of STAFF at work is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(f).

areas.subPointsNote: Headings only by design - not a hospitality exposure.

areas.hospitalityNote: Could touch hotel schools and in-house academies that assess or admit learners.

areas.area: Employment, workers management and access to self-employment
areas.hospitalityNote: The main hotel exposure. 4(a) recruitment and evaluation; 4(b) task allocation by behaviour or traits, performance and behaviour monitoring, decisions on terms, promotion and termination.
areas.headingVerbatim: Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates.
subPoints.hotelUse: CV screening and candidate ranking for seasonal hiring. The single most likely high-risk exposure in hospitality.

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.
subPoints.hotelUse: Shift or room allocation using performance, ratings, punctuality or reliability; housekeeping productivity tracking (output speed is performance, para 275); promotion and termination scoring. Allocation on stated availability alone is outside the task-allocation limb (paras 271-272). AI used exclusively to protect property or for safety, and AI that flags issues only to the worker, are outside (paras 277-278).

areas.area: Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits
areas.hospitalityNote: Only 5(b) creditworthiness and 5(c) life and health insurance pricing. Room, menu and table pricing are NOT listed, and 5(b) is limited to essential private services, which a hotel stay is not (draft guidelines paras 301-304).
areas.headingVerbatim: Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services.
AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud.
subPoints.hotelUse: Draft guidelines tie 5(b) to essential private services: financial resources (accounts, payment services, loans, credit lines, mortgages), housing, electricity, telecoms, possibly health, other utilities and transport (paras 297, 301-303); leisure and travel loans are not essential (para 304). Scoring guests to decide deposits or prepayment for a hotel stay is therefore most likely outside 5(b) (narrowing reading, judgement); long-stay or serviced apartments used as a home could count as housing. Customer classification and personalised marketing are outside (p. 88). Fraud detection is carved out where it is the main intended use (paras 306-308).

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance.
subPoints.hotelUse: The ONLY pricing in Annex III. Room, menu and table pricing are not listed. This is the provision people misread as covering dynamic pricing.

subPoints.text: AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems.

annexI.summary: Route 1 to high-risk: AI that is a safety component of a product already regulated under EU harmonisation law. The Omnibus narrowed this: AI solely used for non-safety-related user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control does not qualify as a safety component, unless failure would endanger health and safety.
annexI.hospitalityNote: Reachable in a hotel via building systems: lifts, machinery, automated doors, pool plant, kitchen machinery. But energy optimisation, convenience automation and quality control are now expressly carved out unless safety-critical - which removes most hotel BMS use from this route.
annexI.omnibusCorrection: Annex I Section A point 1 deleted; Section B gains point 21, Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery. Machinery therefore moved from Section A to Section B, changing its conformity-assessment route and bringing it within the new Art. 60a real-world testing regime.

sections.explanation: Art. 6(1) requires BOTH that the AI is a safety component of (or is itself) an Annex I product AND that the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation. Section A lists New Legislative Framework legislation; Section B lists other harmonisation legislation. The split matters because Art. 43(3) governs the conformity route for Section A, the new Art. 60a governs real-world testing for Section B, and the new Art. 2(13) requirement-limitation is available only where SECTION A legislation gives equivalent protection.

hotelRelevantSectionA.item: Lifts (Directive 2014/33/EU, Annex I Section A point 4)
hotelRelevantSectionA.hotelUse: The clearest Annex I touchpoint in a hotel. AI controlling a lift safety function is a safety component.

Largely neutralised: new Art. 6(1c) provides that a product requiring third-party assessment SOLELY for non-health-and-safety risks, in particular spectrum allocation or electromagnetic interference, does not satisfy Art. 6(1)(b).

movedToSectionB.detail: Annex I Section A point 1 (Directive 2006/42/EC) was DELETED by the Omnibus and machinery added to Section B as point 21 (Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, which repealed 2006/42/EC).
movedToSectionB.hotelUse: Kitchen machinery, laundry equipment, automated doors.
consequences: Section A conformity routing under Art. 43(3) no longer applies to machinery.
Real-world testing of machinery-related high-risk AI now falls under the new Art. 60a regime for Section B, outside AI regulatory sandboxes.
The new Art. 2(13) requirement-limitation is drafted around Section A legislation, so machinery is no longer eligible for it.

sections.netHotelPosition: Combining Art. 6(1a) (AI solely for non-safety purposes is not a safety component), Art. 6(1c) (spectrum and EMI risks do not count) and the machinery move, the practical Annex I exposure for a hotel reduces to safety-critical AI in lifts, gas appliances and pressure equipment. Building-management AI doing energy optimisation, comfort, convenience or quality control is outside the route. This is the research's clearest instance of the Omnibus reducing hotel exposure.

annexI.draftGuidelines: Draft Annex I guidelines (19 May 2026): an AI system is a safety component if it is INTENDED to prevent or mitigate a safety risk, OR if its FAILURE would endanger health, safety or property (paras 37-46). Lift door timing and obstacle detection AI is a safety component even if its intended purpose is efficient operation (para 46). AI optimising gas combustion efficiency can be one if failure could cause carbon monoxide, explosion or fire; AI optimising heating schedules is not (para 43). Smart thermostats and appliances are mostly out; door locks are named as a possible exception (paras 48-49, fn 5). For Section B legislation only Arts. 6(1), 102-109 and 112 apply (para 60). The draft appears to predate the Omnibus move of machinery to Section B (judgement).

NEW: requirements in Arts. 9-15 and 17-25 may be LIMITED for Art. 6(1) Annex I high-risk systems where Annex I Section A law gives equivalent or higher protection, provided overall protection is not reduced. Commission delegated acts due by 2 Aug 2027 to specify scope.
"Safety component" redefined: a component fulfils a safety function where its intended purpose is to prevent or mitigate risks to health and safety. SME (14a) and SMC (14b) definitions inserted.

NEW ARTICLE: processing special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction. Providers of high-risk systems may exceptionally process such data under six cumulative conditions (no viable alternative data, technical limits and pseudonymisation, access controls, no onward transfer, deletion once bias corrected, documented necessity). Para 2 extends the option to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers/deployers of other systems, creating no obligation to do so.

New prohibitions (ba) non-consensual intimate imagery of an identifiable person and (bb) material within Directive 2011/93/EU, subject to a national 'without right' defence. New paras 1a and 1b. All apply from 2 Dec 2026.

enforcementStructure.question: Do the new AI Office powers in Arts. 75a-75d reach hotels?
enforcementStructure.answer: No, not directly. Art. 75(1) as replaced by the Omnibus gives the AI Office EXCLUSIVE competence over (a) AI systems based on general-purpose AI models where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, or by providers in the same undertaking, and (b) AI systems constituting or integrated into a VLOP or VLOSE under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. That exclusive competence applies to the PROVIDERS of those systems, and to deployers only where the deployer is also the provider or part of the same undertaking as the provider.
enforcementStructure.whyHotelsAreOutside: A hotel deploying a vendor's AI is neither the provider nor part of the provider's undertaking. Even a chain that builds its own assistant on a third-party LLM API (scenario P1) is provider of the SYSTEM while the LLM company remains provider of the MODEL - different providers, different undertakings - so Art. 75(1)(a) is not met. Hotels remain supervised by national market surveillance authorities.
enforcementStructure.sectoralExclusions: Art. 75(1)(a) itself carves out: AI related to Annex I products; Annex III point 2 (critical infrastructure); systems provided by law enforcement, border management and financial institutions under Art. 74(6); and Annex III point 8 as regards administration of justice.

twoIndirectChannels.channel: As the regime facing your vendors
twoIndirectChannels.detail: The AI Office's new powers - investigations, remote and on-site inspections, document and data access, sealing of premises, orders to provide access and explanations, retention obligations, appointment of external auditors, and full cost recovery from non-compliant operators - apply to the GPAI-based system providers hotels buy from. Art. 75b lets the AI Office make an operator's commitments binding; Art. 75c allows non-compliance decisions, fines under Art. 99(3)-(7) applied mutatis mutandis, and periodic penalty payments. A vendor under AI Office proceedings is a continuity risk to its hotel customers.

New Art. 75(2a) lets a market surveillance authority with well-founded and sufficient reasons to suspect an infringement ask the AI Office, through the Art. 70(2) single point of contact, to assess the matter. The AI Office must respond within four months stating whether it will exercise its Art. 75a powers. This is the route by which a hotel matter could reach the AI Office indirectly.

enforcementStructure.newReportingRoute: Art. 75(1a): providers within the AI Office's competence report serious incidents to the AI Office rather than under Art. 73. Not a hotel duty, but it changes where a vendor's incident reports go.

Per the draft guidelines (paras 73-74), corporate-account credit checks are outside 5(b), including where an owner is assessed to back a company loan, because the primary beneficiary is the company. So the practical FRIA trigger for a hotel is narrow.

draftClassificationGuidelines.coverageCaveat: All three drafts read by 13 Nov 2026: General principles in full; Annex I safety-component test (paras 23-62); Annex III horizontal issues (paras 69-93), biometrics (paras 119-177), employment (paras 236-278 and examples) and credit scoring 5(b) (paras 294-309 and examples). draftClassificationGuidelines.sourceParagraphs: Paragraph numbers below are the draft Annex III document's own numbering.

horizontalFindings.topic: Human involvement does not change classification
horizontalFindings.finding: For Art. 6(2), the only relevant determinant is whether the intended purpose includes an Annex III use case. Human involvement cannot change the purpose, so it has no effect on classification. Human oversight is a compliance requirement under Art. 14, not a classification escape. A provider cannot categorise a system as low risk simply by adding a human-involvement requirement.
horizontalFindings.qualification: Human involvement can matter, but only as evidence that the tasks are narrow procedural, preparatory, or improve a previously completed human activity - i.e. only inside the Art. 6(3) filter.

horizontalFindings.topic: Art. 6(3) filter must be read narrowly
horizontalFindings.finding: The filter is an exception to rules protecting fundamental rights, so its conditions must be interpreted narrowly and in light of the opening requirement that the system not materially influence the outcome of the decision.

horizontalFindings.topic: Narrow procedural task has a hard edge
horizontalFindings.finding: Covers categorising, reformatting, restructuring or re-presenting data, and changing metadata. It does NOT cover systems that perform a value judgement on data relevant for decision-making.

horizontalFindings.topic: Split architectures and agentic systems are assessed as a whole
horizontalFindings.finding: Where several AI systems form a complex system whose combined intended purpose or joint outputs materially influence an individual decision, the whole configuration is treated as a single AI system for classification, expressly to prevent circumvention by design. This extends to agentic systems coordinating through linked actions. A module that would qualify for the Art. 6(3) filter on its own loses it where the overall configuration influences key aspects of decisions in a high-risk use case. Genuinely separable components put into service independently that do not contribute to a high-risk purpose stay out of scope.
horizontalFindings.hotelRelevance: A chain stitching an assistant together from an LLM, PMS and CRM connectors, or running agentic workflows, is classified on the whole assembly, not component by component.

horizontalFindings.topic: Intended purpose is assessed before placing on the market
horizontalFindings.finding: Intended use equals the intended purpose as defined by the provider. The system need not actually be in use; the provider must assess intended use before placing on the market or putting into service, and conformity must exist at that moment.

horizontalFindings.topic: Natural versus legal persons narrows credit scoring
horizontalFindings.finding: Annex III 5(b) covers creditworthiness of natural persons. A system assessing companies from business data, balance sheets and financial statements is out of scope. Critically, where the owner of a legal entity is assessed to back a company loan, the owner does NOT fall under 5(b), because the primary beneficiary of the credit is the company, not the individual. Sole traders and the self-employed assessed in their own right ARE natural persons.
horizontalFindings.hotelRelevance: Corporate-account credit checks are outside Annex III 5(b). Scoring an individual guest, or a sole trader in their own right, is inside it.

employmentFindings.topic: Personal scope reaches far beyond employees
employmentFindings.finding: Point 4 covers employment, workers' management AND access to self-employment. Work-related contractual relationships are not limited to formal employment contracts. Freelancers, independent professionals, service providers, solo self-employed persons in situations comparable to workers, and platform workers regardless of contractual status all fall within scope wherever AI systems mediate or condition their access to work opportunities. Workplace is interpreted broadly, including virtual spaces.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: HIGH. Hospitality runs on agency staff, extras, seasonal contractors, freelance F&B and events crew and platform-sourced labour. An AI system selecting or allocating among those populations is in scope even though none of them is an employee. The research currently frames point 4 around employees and understates this.

employmentFindings.topic: A human signing off does not take a decision out of 4(b)
employmentFindings.finding: Decisions is read functionally, not formalistically: any act or omission attributable to the employer producing material effects on the worker's contractual position or the modalities of their work. It expressly includes both fully automated decisions AND cases where a human operator formally decides but significantly relies on the AI output. Omissions count, including a failure to promote.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Removes the 'our manager always reviews it' defence as a classification argument. It remains relevant to Art. 14 compliance, not to whether the system is high-risk.

employmentFindings.topic: Working time and leave are terms of the relationship
employmentFindings.finding: Terms of work-related relationships are the fundamental elements of the contract or relationship, including pay entitlements, working time arrangements, leave rights and resting periods. Decisions on them extend beyond formal contract changes to determinations materially affecting enjoyment of those rights. The guidelines give two express examples: denial of a leave request, and a significant change to regular working hours.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: VERY HIGH and not in the research. Rota and workforce-management software that significantly changes regular working hours, or that decides leave requests, is within point 4(b) regardless of whether it allocates by performance. The research frames D5 around performance-based allocation and monitoring; the working-time and leave dimension is a separate and probably larger hospitality exposure.

employmentFindings.finding: Not every operational adjustment reaches point 4(b). The decision must reach a threshold of significance; determinations that do not materially alter rights or obligations under the contract fall outside. Express example of what is OUT: allocation of office space, and of break or lunch timing within an assigned shift, so long as the worker's total break and lunch time does not change.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: This is the usable line for the research's open question about allocating shifts by availability alone. Sequencing tasks within an already-assigned shift without altering total rest entitlement sits below the threshold; changing the shift pattern itself does not. Separately, the open question about allocating shifts by availability alone is answered by paras 271-272 (finding e9).

employmentFindings.topic: AI-driven non-renewal of a fixed-term contract is termination
employmentFindings.finding: Termination covers dismissal, redundancy, and non-renewal of fixed-term contracts where the decision not to renew is AI-driven, plus any act of equivalent effect. Non-definitive removals from work may qualify as material modifications of terms.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: MAJOR and absent from the research. Seasonal hospitality runs on fixed-term contracts. The research identifies seasonal hiring as the principal exposure through recruitment under 4(a); this adds the other end of the season - AI-influenced decisions about who is not brought back - as a 4(b) termination case.

employmentFindings.finding: Training entitlement is an essential aspect of the employment relationship. Optional or ancillary training with no entitlement and no legal or collectively agreed obligation does not automatically fall in point 4(b). But where completion or assessment conditions advancement, promotion, remuneration, grade or continued employability, an AI system evaluating performance in training modules falls within 4(b).
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Chain e-learning and certification platforms with AI assessment are common. Whether they are in scope turns on whether completion gates progression or continued employment.

employmentFindings.topic: A prohibition beats a high-risk classification
employmentFindings.finding: Where a system falls within both Art. 5 and Annex III point 4, the prohibition prevails and the system is unlawful irrespective of any safeguards by provider or deployer. Recital 44 grounds the workplace emotion-recognition prohibition in the structural power imbalance between employers and workers or candidates.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Confirms the research's handling of D7: no compliance programme rescues staff emotion recognition.

employmentFindings.finding: For 4(a), the activity must relate to or impact the substance of the recruitment process, covering preparatory steps - targeted advertising, prospecting, pre-application screening - and the selection process - shortlisting, grading, ranking, testing. An AI system that exclusively generates job descriptions from tasks and qualifications already defined by a human recruiter is treated as performing a narrow procedural task, but job-description and advertisement tools can fall within 4(a) where their intended purpose plays a role in recruitment affecting applicants' prospects, particularly given that biased drafting can increase discrimination risk.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Prospecting and pre-application screening are wider than the research's current framing. The job-description nuance matters because writing seasonal job ads with a general chatbot is routine in hotels and sits close to the line.

employmentFindings.topic: Availability and accreditation are objective criteria
employmentFindings.finding: Task allocation relying only on objective, neutral, external criteria tied to job requirements - availability indicated by workers, a required accreditation, geographical proximity - is outside the task-allocation limb of 4(b). Such criteria cannot be proxies for nationality or ethnicity.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Rota or room allocation on stated availability alone is not high-risk task allocation. Working-time changes and leave decisions remain under e3.

employmentFindings.finding: Punctuality, responsiveness to customer requests, reliability metrics and performance ratings are personal traits or characteristics. Worked example: a retail/logistics scheduler using punctuality, no-show history, shift acceptance and customer/manager ratings to rank and auto-allocate shifts is high-risk and cannot use Art. 6(3).
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: The closest Commission example to hotel rota tools.

employmentFindings.topic: Monitoring is a stand-alone category; speed is performance
employmentFindings.finding: Monitor and evaluate are alternatives; the category applies whether or not pay or hours change. Performance includes quantitative measures such as tasks completed or output speed, and AI ratings that feed employee files.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Housekeeping rooms-per-hour tracking reported to supervisors is high-risk.

employmentFindings.topic: Exclusions: legal duty, safety, asset protection, worker-only feedback
employmentFindings.finding: AI used exclusively to meet legal obligations, for medical or safety reasons, or to protect property and company assets is outside 4(b), unless also used to evaluate staff. AI that flags issues only to the worker, not to the employer, is not high-risk. Voluntary training feedback only to the employee is outside.
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Shrink detection, security tools and coaching feedback to the attendant or cook only stay out. This is a narrowing reading where it relies on 'only to the worker'; check the actual reporting flow.

employmentFindings.finding: Flagging an imminent fixed-term contract lapse without evaluation or suggestion is not high-risk (para 266). AI that only compiles attendance records into reports, with no scoring or flags, falls in 4(b) but benefits from the Art. 6(3)(d) preparatory-task filter (example p. 78).
employmentFindings.hotelRelevance: Narrowing readings: do not bank until final.

draftClassificationGuidelines.secondConsultation: General principles para 5: the draft 'will be further consulted with the AI Board and published for additional stakeholder feedback before the Guidelines are adopted'. The end-2026 target may slip (judgement).
draftClassificationGuidelines.outdatedPoint: General principles para 449 still dates the Art. 111(2) cut-off as 'before 2 August 2026'. Superseded: the Omnibus replaced Art. 111(2) with the date of application of Chapter III (2 Dec 2027 for Annex III, 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I). The Omnibus recital adds that the grace period applies per type and model already placed on the market, as long as the design is unchanged.

generalPrincipleFindings.topic: The vendor's description sets the intended purpose
generalPrincipleFindings.finding: If instructions, terms, marketing or documentation present a general system as broadly applicable and do not consistently limit or exclude high-risk uses, its intended purpose is deemed to include them; a terms-of-service exclusion alone is insufficient.
generalPrincipleFindings.hotelRelevance: Read the vendor's intended-purpose statement when buying HR or workforce tools; it decides classification.

generalPrincipleFindings.finding: The assessment of whether a system is intended for a high-risk use is the provider's responsibility, supervised by market surveillance authorities.
The Commission is preparing separate guidelines on responsibilities along the AI value chain under Art. 25, with more detail on the three routes by which others become providers.

biometricFindings.topic: 1:1 verification and opt-in access control are outside
biometricFindings.finding: Verification against a document chip, ID card, device or a database encrypted with a key held only by the person is outside high-risk. Access control where registered persons consciously present themselves is not remote, even one-to-many against registered people. Informing people of a system is not active involvement.

Identifying a person from CCTV on private property without their active involvement is remote biometric identification; point 1(a) is not limited to publicly accessible spaces. An entry check where the person steps in front of the camera is not remote.

A private company's voice database can be a reference database; voiceprint matching without active involvement is remote identification. Calling a bank's customer service and authenticating by voice is verification.
biometricFindings.hotelRelevance: Hotel voice agents that recognise returning callers by voiceprint, without opt-in, are high-risk.

biometricFindings.finding: Call-centre AI inferring customers' emotions from vocal tone, pitch and volume - for satisfaction statistics or to route angry callers to a human - is high-risk emotion recognition, whether or not it identifies the customer. Crowd-mood cameras are also covered. Text sentiment, smiles alone, pain and fatigue are not emotion recognition.
biometricFindings.hotelRelevance: A new hotel exposure: voice agents and call analytics with guest-emotion features are high-risk from 2 Dec 2027; deployers must inform callers (Art. 50(3)).

biometricFindings.topic: Age and gender inference are not 1(b)
biometricFindings.finding: Age estimation and gender inference are not high-risk under 1(b) because age and gender are not GDPR Art. 9 attributes.

creditFindings.topic: 5(b) is limited to essential private services
creditFindings.finding: Creditworthiness or credit scoring is high-risk where used for access to financial resources or essential services: bank accounts, payment services, loans and credit lines, mortgages, housing, electricity, telecoms, possibly health, other utilities and transport. Leisure and travel loans, premium credit cards and complex financial instruments are not essential.
creditFindings.hotelRelevance: Guest deposit or prepayment scoring for hotel stays is most likely outside 5(b). Long-stay or serviced apartments used as a home could count as housing (judgement).
creditFindings.posture: Narrowing reading grounded in recital 58; downgraded the hotel example but kept on the watch list.

creditFindings.finding: Fraud detection must be the main intended use; then the system is outside 5(b) even if outputs feed a credit decision. AML/CFT systems are not covered by the carve-out.
Classifying customers for information, suitability or personalised marketing is outside 5(b) unless part of a creditworthiness assessment.

interimPostures.purpose: Three open items cannot be settled by research: they depend on external events. Rather than leaving them blank, each carries a stated position to proceed on, the trigger that would change it, and which scenarios move if it does. postures.subject: Final Commission guidelines on high-risk classification
postures.currentState: Draft published 19 May 2026. Consultation closed 23 July 2026. The Commission states the final version will be adopted by the end of 2026. Non-binding even when final; only the CJEU gives the authoritative reading. Update 13 Nov 2026: the general-principles draft says it will be further consulted with the AI Board and published for additional stakeholder feedback before adoption (para 5), so the end-2026 target may slip.
postures.posture: Proceed on the draft as the Commission's current reading, applied ASYMMETRICALLY: adopt the draft's exposure-WIDENING interpretations now, and do not bank its exposure-NARROWING interpretations as settled.
postures.rationale: The draft is the best available evidence of how market surveillance authorities will approach Art. 6, and the Commission is unlikely to retreat from positions grounded in recitals and CJEU case law. But a narrowing reading that disappears in the final version leaves a hotel non-compliant, whereas a widening reading that is relaxed leaves it merely over-prepared. The costs of being wrong are not symmetric, so the treatment should not be either.
adoptNow: Point 4's personal scope reaches freelancers, agency staff, contractors and platform workers (e1)
A human formally deciding while significantly relying on AI output does not escape 4(b) (e2)
Working time changes and leave decisions are terms of the work-related relationship (e3)
AI-driven non-renewal of a fixed-term contract is termination (e5)
Split architectures and agentic assemblies are classified as a whole (g4)
The Art. 6(3) filter is to be read narrowly (g2)
Guest emotion recognition from voice in call handling is high-risk (b4)
Private-property CCTV identification is remote biometric identification (b2)
Behavioural indicators and output speed bring allocation and monitoring into 4(b) (e10, e11)
doNotBank: The day-to-day threshold that puts within-shift task sequencing outside 4(b) (e4)
The narrow-procedural-task treatment of job-description generation (e8)
The exclusion of corporate-account credit assessment from 5(b) (g6)
Guest deposit scoring outside 5(b) because hotel stays are not an essential private service (c1)
