postures.trigger: Adoption of the final guidelines, expected by end 2026. Secondary trigger: any CJEU ruling on Art. 6.
postures.ifItChanges: Re-read the final version against the six adopted positions above. If any is dropped, the affected scenario classifications loosen and the data file's confidence levels on those entries should rise from draft-guidance. If new widening positions appear, D4, D5, P2 and P3 are the scenarios to re-test first.
postures.timelineFit: Likely to land inside the SBP timeline. This is the one of the three worth actively watching.

postures.subject: EU-US Data Privacy Framework validity
postures.currentState: DPF valid as of 10 Nov 2026. Latombe's appeal (C-703/25 P) is pending at the Court of Justice with no hearing date scheduled. Three further pressure points: the US Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter (29 Jun 2026) allowing at-will removal of FTC members; pending litigation over the removal of PCLOB members, an oversight body for the DPF's intelligence safeguards; and the expiry of FISA Section 702's statutory authorisation in June 2026, with collection reported to continue under court certifications through March 2027. noyb asked the Commission to repeal the framework on 30 June 2026 and signalled its own annulment action.
postures.posture: Treat the DPF as valid but unreliable as a sole transfer basis. Keep standard contractual clauses and transfer impact assessments in place as a live fallback, not a contingency document. Prefer EU-hosted AI for guest and staff personal data, and for any special-category data treat EU hosting as the default rather than the preference.
postures.rationale: This is the research's existing posture, extended. The practical point for a hotel is that invalidation is a vendor-switching problem, not a paperwork problem: a mid-contract DPF collapse means either the vendor can host in the EU or the hotel stops using it. That makes the actionable step contractual and architectural, taken before any ruling, rather than legal analysis afterwards.

decisionRules.if: CJEU invalidates the adequacy decision in C-703/25 P
decisionRules.then: DPF ceases to be a lawful transfer basis. SCCs plus TIAs become the only route, and every existing TIA must be redone, because the CJEU's findings on US surveillance would be the very premise the old assessments relied on. Any AI vendor processing EU personal data on US infrastructure needs an EU hosting option or replacement.

decisionRules.if: The Commission repeals or suspends the framework following noyb's request or political pressure
decisionRules.then: Same operational consequence, possibly with a transition period. Watch for a Commission statement specifying wind-down terms.

decisionRules.if: noyb files and the cases are joined
decisionRules.then: No immediate operational change, but the timeline compresses and the probability of invalidation rises, because a fresh case can be built around Trump v. Slaughter, which the General Court was never asked about.

decisionRules.if: FISA 702 collection authority lapses after March 2027 without reauthorisation
decisionRules.then: Reduces one surveillance concern but destabilises the framework's legal architecture; monitor rather than act.
The DPF survives this challenge but not the political risk. Maintain SCCs and TIAs regardless; do not treat dismissal as closure.

postures.scenarioNote: P1 is the sharpest: a chain's own assistant built on a non-EU LLM API is a continuous transfer of guest data. D1 is a vendor-processor question. P5 concerns training data rather than live transfers.
postures.timelineFit: Almost certainly will NOT settle inside the SBP timeline - no hearing date has been set. State the posture and move on.

postures.subject: Art. 2(13) delegated acts limiting Arts. 9-15 and 17-25
postures.currentState: New Art. 2(13) permits the application of Arts. 9-15 and 17-25 to be limited for Art. 6(1) Annex I high-risk systems where Annex I Section A legislation provides equivalent or higher protection and overall protection is not reduced. The Commission must adopt delegated acts by 2 August 2027 specifying which systems, which obligations, the conditions and the scope. Nothing has been specified yet.
postures.posture: Assume NO limitation. Plan full compliance with Arts. 9-15 and 17-25 for any Annex I high-risk system until a delegated act says otherwise.
postures.rationale: The limitation is discretionary relief, not a duty, and its scope is entirely unspecified. Planning for full compliance and later receiving relief wastes preparation; planning for relief that does not arrive leaves a system non-compliant at the 2 Aug 2028 deadline. The asymmetry is obvious and the choice is not close.
postures.mitigatingFactor: This matters less for hospitality than it first appears. After the new Art. 6(1a) carve-out for non-safety-related AI and Art. 6(1c) for spectrum and EMI risks, a hotel's Annex I exposure reduces to safety-critical AI in lifts, gas appliances and pressure equipment. Machinery moved to Annex I Section B, and Art. 2(13) is drafted around Section A, so machinery is not eligible for this relief at all.
postures.trigger: Adoption of delegated acts under Art. 97, due by 2 Aug 2027. A public consultation would likely precede them.
postures.ifItChanges: Identify whether any limitation covers lifts (Directive 2014/33/EU), gas appliances (Regulation (EU) 2016/426) or pressure equipment (Directive 2014/68/EU). If none does, nothing changes for hotels. If one does, the affected provider obligations in obligationsByRoleAndTier may be reduced for that system class only.
postures.scenarioNote: None of the 13 scenarios is an Annex I case, so no scenario moves. This is a completeness item, not an exposure item.
postures.timelineFit: Due 2 Aug 2027, after the SBP ends. Lowest priority of the three.

nationalLayer.scopeNote: Four focus countries are EU Member States, where the AI Act applies directly but each state must designate national authorities (Art. 70). The UK and Switzerland are outside the EU: the AI Act has no national layer there, but it still reaches UK and Swiss hotel groups that place AI on the EU market or whose AI output is used in the EU, for example at EU properties (Art. 2).
nationalLayer.keyFinding: For hotels, the sharper national constraint is labour law, not AI Act enforcement. In every focus country with a works-council or union regime, staff-facing AI (rostering, performance tracking, CV screening) triggers information, consultation or co-determination duties before it is introduced - in Germany and France, courts can stop the rollout.

commissionList.name: Commission list of market surveillance authorities under the AI Act

countries.aiActAuthority: Bundesnetzagentur (Federal Network Agency): market surveillance authority, single point of contact under Art. 70(2) and central complaints body under Art. 85. Hybrid model: sectoral regulators keep their existing product areas, with the Bundesnetzagentur coordinating.
countries.legalBasis: KI-Marktueberwachungs- und Innovationsfoerderungsgesetz (KI-MIG), in force 29 July 2026.
countries.labourRules: Works Constitution Act (BetrVG): the works council co-determines the introduction of technical systems capable of monitoring employee behaviour or performance (s. 87(1) no. 6), which covers most AI rostering, performance and HR tools; it must be informed of planned AI use (s. 90); it co-determines selection guidelines, including where AI is used (s. 95(2a)); and it may call in an AI expert (s. 80(3)). Introduction without agreement can be stopped by injunction.
countries.hotelNote: A hotel with a works council cannot unilaterally switch on monitoring-capable AI such as performance-based shift allocation or housekeeping productivity tracking (scenario D5).

countries.aiActAuthority: DGCCRF: coordinator of the market surveillance authorities and single point of contact under Art. 70(2). Under the government's scheme the CNIL would supervise most Annex III systems, including employment (point 4) and biometrics (point 1); the ACPR creditworthiness (5(b)) where the operator falls under it; and the DGCCRF with Arcom the Art. 50 chatbot and synthetic-content duties.
countries.legalBasis: Projet de loi DDADUE (various EU-law adaptation provisions): adopted by the Senate at first reading on 18 Feb 2026, still before the Assemblee nationale in October 2026.
countries.designationStatus: Pending. DGCCRF is notified to the Commission as single point of contact; the sectoral allocation, including the CNIL's role for employment AI, is not yet law.
countries.labourRules: Code du travail art. L2312-8 II 4: in firms with 50 or more employees the CSE must be informed and consulted on the introduction of new technologies, before the employer decides (L2312-14); failure is the offence of obstruction (delit d'entrave, L2317-1). Courts in 2025-2026 suspended AI deployments pending consultation; the Paris Court of Appeal (21 May 2026) held that a pilot phase is not exempt and that authorising and regulating by charter a tool staff already used counts as introducing it.
countries.hotelNote: Directly relevant to shadow AI: once a hotel group authorises, or writes a usage charter for, a chatbot staff already use, it must consult the CSE first.

countries.aiActAuthority: AESIA (Agencia Espanola de Supervision de la Inteligencia Artificial): operational and notified to the Commission as market surveillance authority and single point of contact. The AEPD has said it can already act against prohibited AI that involves personal data under data-protection law.
countries.legalBasis: AESIA statute: Royal Decree 729/2023. The organic AI governance bill (approved by the Council of Ministers on 26 May 2026) lapsed when the Cortes were dissolved on 6 Oct 2026; general elections are on 29 Nov 2026.
countries.designationStatus: Provisional. No national implementing law; the bill must be reintroduced in the next legislature.
countries.labourRules: Estatuto de los Trabajadores art. 64.4(d), added by Ley 12/2021 (the Rider Law): the works council has the right to be informed of the parameters, rules and instructions on which algorithms or AI systems are based where they affect working conditions or access to and retention of employment, including profiling. It applies to all employers, not only platforms.
countries.hotelNote: A Spanish hotel using algorithmic scheduling, CV screening or performance scoring must be able to explain the system's logic to its works council.

countries.aiActAuthority: Post- och telestyrelsen (PTS): notified to the Commission as market surveillance authority and single point of contact. Pending supplementary legislation, PTS and other authorities hold a government mandate to act as national competent authorities until 31 Dec 2026.
countries.legalBasis: Inquiry SOU 2025:101 proposed a supplementary act with PTS as coordinating authority among eleven market surveillance authorities. PTS describes the supplementary Swedish legislation as still awaited.
countries.designationStatus: Interim mandate to 31 Dec 2026; supplementary law pending.
countries.labourRules: Co-determination Act (MBL) s. 11: before deciding an important change to the business or to working or employment conditions, the employer must on its own initiative negotiate with the union; ss. 11-14 set the negotiation duty and breach can lead to damages. The rule is not AI-specific: whether a given AI rollout is an important change is a judgement.
countries.hotelNote: Introducing AI rostering or performance tools in a Swedish hotel with a collective agreement should be treated as requiring prior MBL negotiation.

countries.aiActAuthority: None. The EU AI Act is not UK law. It still reaches a UK group that places AI on the EU market or whose AI output is used in the EU (Art. 2), for example at EU properties.
countries.legalBasis: No AI-specific statute. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s. 80, replaced UK GDPR Art. 22 with Arts. 22A-22D from 5 Feb 2026: solely automated decisions with significant effects are permitted with safeguards (information, representations, human intervention, contest), except where based on special-category data, where the prohibition remains.
countries.labourRules: The ICO leads on AI in recruitment through data-protection law; its recruitment guidance is under review after the 2025 Act and new automated decision-making guidance is in consultation in 2026.
countries.hotelNote: UK properties face a looser automated-decision rule than EU properties under GDPR Art. 22, but EU properties of the same group remain under the AI Act and the EU GDPR.

countries.aiActAuthority: None. Switzerland has no AI act. The EU AI Act still reaches Swiss groups that place AI on the EU market or whose AI output is used in the EU (Art. 2).
countries.legalBasis: Federal Council decision of 12 Feb 2025: ratify the Council of Europe AI Convention (signed 27 Mar 2025) and adapt law sector by sector; the consultation on the draft act is scheduled for spring 2027 (Federal Council, 28 Oct 2026); it will cover transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, supervision and risk assessment. Revised Data Protection Act art. 21: a person must be informed of a decision based solely on automated processing that has legal effects or significantly affects them, and can ask for human review.
countries.designationStatus: Consultation on the draft act scheduled for spring 2027 (Federal Council press release, 28 Oct 2026). Non-binding track: OFCOM 'Guide on an AI Code of Conduct' (26 Oct 2026), a ten-article template for voluntary AI codes of associations and companies.
countries.labourRules: Ordinance 3 to the Labour Act (ArGV 3) art. 26: monitoring or control systems intended to monitor employees' behaviour at the workplace are prohibited; where needed for other reasons they must not impair health or freedom of movement. The Federal Supreme Court (BGE 130 II 425) reads this as not a general ban on technical monitoring.
countries.hotelNote: AI that tracks the behaviour of housekeeping or front-desk staff runs into ArGV 3 art. 26 whatever happens on AI-specific law.

transparencyGuidelines.document: Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 AI Act, C(2026) 7702 final
transparencyGuidelines.status: Final. Not binding; only the CJEU gives the authoritative reading (para 5).

findings.topic: Who is provider and who is deployer
findings.finding: A company that builds an interactive AI system in-house and uses it under its own name is the provider; modifying another provider's generative system with new training data and putting it into service under its own name also makes it provider. The deployer is whoever decides to deploy the system and how it is used; technical control is not needed, including in group corporate structures. A company that commissions an advertising agency without deciding how it uses AI is not the deployer.

Staff using AI assistance to communicate with people is indirect interaction and outside Art. 50(1). Blended services need disclosure for AI outputs unless these are properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors.

AI agents that make bookings, manage correspondence or conclude contracts must disclose that they are AI and on whose behalf they act, including in multi-agent set-ups, and to the persons instructing them at key steps.

First-turn text disclosure, spoken statement at the start of calls with reminders in longer interactions, persistent labels; tones alone are insufficient; disclosures only in terms and conditions, URLs or documentation are insufficient; account for children, the elderly and persons with disabilities.

Interpreted restrictively. Covers e.g. internal assistants for trained, AI-literate staff (HR, legal, procurement, IT). Does not cover customer or helpdesk chatbots, realistic avatars or human-like voices.

Recommenders, spam filters, translation and transcription tools, search without content generation, authentication and biometric recognition systems, predictive maintenance, product visualisation (incl. room staging). Interacting (humanoid) robots and cobots are in scope.

Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and Consumer Rights Directive duties apply regardless of whether the AI interaction is obvious; an AI-driven service can be a main characteristic to disclose before contract.
Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must inform all persons exposed, including children, at the latest at first exposure, e.g. by notices at entrances or onboarding messages.

An AI-generated product image that misleads as to the product's actual appearance, characteristics or use is a deep fake. A real product shown against an AI-generated background is not, if not misleading. Colour correction, background extension, removing passers-by and similar minor edits are not deep fakes.
findings.hotelRelevance: AI images that make rooms, views or facilities look better than they are must be labelled and remain misleading under consumer law.

findings.topic: Text on matters of public interest
findings.finding: Ad copy and product descriptions are outside the Art. 50(4) text duty, except claims related to health, consumer safety or sustainability; corporate reports on a listed company's website are in scope. Exception only with substantive human review including fact-checking and a person holding editorial responsibility; spell-checks, policies or cursory approval do not qualify; AI changes after sign-off void the exception.
findings.hotelRelevance: AI-written sustainability claims and published ESG or investor reports.

findings.finding: Art. 50 applies from 2 Aug 2026 to all in-scope systems whatever their launch date; only Art. 50(2) marking for generative systems placed before 2 Aug 2026 has a transition to 2 Dec 2026. Content generated before 2 Aug 2026 need not be labelled retroactively, but older public-interest text published after that date must be. The Art. 111(2) high-risk grandfathering does not cover Art. 50 duties.
Up to EUR 15m or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher; for SMEs whichever is lower; authorities consider SMEs' and SMCs' economic viability.
